newsitem.title: KENYA: Drought, disease threaten Kenya coffee crop.
newsitem.headline: Drought, disease threaten Kenya coffee crop.

text.p: Coffee berry disease (CBD) in Kenya's key growing areas in June-July last year and drought have hit production for 1996/97 and more damage is expected, industry officials said on Thursday.
They said the problem of CBD was severe in June-July last year when the weather was wet and humid but the disease no longer posed a threat to Kenyan coffee bushes.
Dr Peter Michori, researcher and director of Kenya's Coffee Research Foundation (CRF), told Reuters the problem now facing the industry was severe drought ravaging the region.
"The disease is no longer the problem, drought is," Michori told Reuters by telephone from a key growing farm at Ruiru, 60 km (40 miles) from Nairobi, where the CRF is based.
Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi has declared the drought a national disaster and appealed for food aid.
Most of Kenya's coffee trees are in their pruning period. Coffee beans are normally harvested from May to August and October to December.
"It really depends on how farmers manage individual farms. Well managed farms produce two harvests," Michori said.

Referring to the coffee berry disease outbreak of last year, a leading trader said, "In many cases the large-scale farmers waited for too long and then when they sprayed (farms), it was all washed off by the rain, which frustated their efforts."
The trader said small-scale farmers suffered the most as they could not afford the spraying materials.

In its third revision of the 1996/97 crop estimates, the Coffee Board of Kenya last month forecast production at 85,000 tonnes in 1996/97 compared to a final figure of 97,575 tonnes in 1995/96 and 95,806 tonnes in 1994/95.
"Drought has added a new dimension to our production jitters. But the board has not offered another production revision yet," an official at a major coffee house said.
He added, "The crop on the trees right now will be affected by drought because it has been persistently dry, so you could see production forecasts reduced again."

Traders said coffee prices would rise internally at Nairobi's weekly export auction based on weather jitters indicating a tight supply equation. But they discounted a dramatic rise saying that depended on global market trends.
Kenya exported 109,372 tonnes of coffee in 1995/96 -- including carryover stocks -- for 16.36 billion shillings ($302.9 million) compared to 79,482 tonnes in 1994/95 worth 14.4 billion shillings.
The coffee board has so far not given export estimates for 1996/97.
